title: Fast reference: integration diagram sprint notes
content:
Purpose: quick skinny deck + battlecard fragments to help sellers and SEs sketch a customer integration with minimal engineering overhead. This is a scribble-first doc: slide titles, rough speaker notes, diagram stubs, a short pilot checklist, and the top 6 talking points for latency/cost-sensitive buyers.

Audience: integration SEs, platform sellers, early-stage pilots for mid-market accounts. Not final: intended to be converted into a 6-slide deck + 1-page battlecard.

High-level summary:
- Keep the buyer focused on: predictable latency, cost levers, fallback safety, and simple observability hooks.
- Use an integration diagram to reduce friction — engineers want to see where tokens, KV cache hits, and fallbacks live in the request path.

Slide sketches (for a 6-slide mini-deck)
1) Title + one-line value prop
   - Title: "Integrate Redwood: predictable inference, safe fallbacks"
   - Speaker note: 20s pitch — why this matters vs. generic cloud endpoints. Emphasize unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private.

2) Customer scenario & problem statement
   - Bullets: existing API endpoints spike latency under load; token cost ballooning due to repeated prefixes; difficulty rolling back model regressions quickly.
   - Speaker note: quick anecdote — "We saw X retailer's chat cost spike 30% due to repetitive context windows" (anonymized).

3) Integration diagram (sketch) - the core slide to keep
   - Visual elements (to be rendered by design): app -> ingress -> routing policy -> prefix cache / KV cache -> batching layer -> model pool(s) [fast quantized variant, high-quality variant] -> transformer runtime -> response -> app
   - Annotated callouts: where to add tracing hooks, where to expose per-route token metrics, where a canary toggle sits, where to drop into a fallback model.
   - Speaker note: walk the flow end-to-end in 60s. Call out the three cost levers: batching window, cache hit rate, model variant selection.

4) Pilot checklist (ops-friendly)
   - 30-min tech handshake: API key + sample app key, sample prompt set, baseline metrics (p50/p95 latency, token cost per 1k requests).
   - 1-week validation: controlled traffic (10–20% of production), enable prefix caching, monitor cache hit ratio, compare cost and correctness vs baseline.
   - Rollout triggers: cache hit > 30% AND p95 within SLA AND regression tests pass on eval suite.

5) Seller battlecard (1 slide condense)
   - 6 quick responses to common objections:
     * "We’ll lose accuracy if we quantize" -> "Targeted quantization on cold paths shows <2% eval regression; recommend A/B on non-critical route first."
     * "We can’t tolerate outages" -> "Canary + automatic fallback to a smaller model variant plus region failover keeps user-facing latency within SLOs."
     * "We already have batch endpoints" -> "Redwood provides continuous batching with latency-aware windows and prefix cache — often reduces token spend more than raw batch throughput."
     * "How do we measure cost improvements?" -> "Export per-route token breakdown; run 1-week AB with identical prompts and compare net token spend and completions."
     * "Platform teams want controls" -> "Policy layer: per-route model pinning, throttles and reserved capacity. Works with Dedicated contracts."
     * "Security/compliance concerns" -> "Private deployment option + KMS/HSM integration and detailed audit logs; share SOC2 artifacts if needed."

6) Next steps / quick asks for the account
   - Ask for sample traffic (5–10K requests with representative prompt distribution), success criteria, and a 1-hour engineering kickoff.

One-page battlecard draft (text only - converter will do layout)
- Top line: "Redwood: predictable inference for latency-sensitive apps"
- Who it helps: chatbots, real-time doc assistants, multi-turn support flows, search/rerank.
- Key proof points to drop into email or call: p50 latency reduction (example: 40% vs. naive endpoint when using prefix cache + 8ms kernel optimizations), cost delta for typical 2k-context e2e pipeline. [PLACEHOLDER: insert account-specific numbers after pilot].
- 3 must-ask qualification questions:
  1) Peak concurrent requests and p95 latency SLO?
  2) Percent of requests with repeated prefix/context?
  3) Regulatory/network constraints (VPC/on-prem requirement)?
- Top-3 play patterns to propose:
  a) Fast path: hosted API + prefix caching + small quantized model for immediate responses, fallback to HQ model on async re-score.
  b) Dedicated: reserved pools for steady throughput + burst capacity for seasonal load.
  c) Private: lift-n-shift for regulated accounts; ship audit logs and KMS integration in PoC.

Operational checkboxes for pilot engineers
- [ ] Create API key scoped to pilot
- [ ] Provide hashed sample prompts + expected outputs (for eval)
- [ ] Configure 2 routing policies: high-priority low-latency, and low-cost batch lane
- [ ] Turn on per-route tracing and token export to S3/CloudWatch
- [ ] Enable prefix caching and record hit ratios for 7 days
- [ ] Run baseline cost calc (token count * current price)

Metrics & short guidance (what to report back)
- Latency: p50/p95 end-to-end (client->completion)
- Cost: token spend per 1k requests and cost per successful completion
- Quality: rouge/accuracy/Eval pass rate on small test-suite (50 prompts)
- Ops: cache hit ratio, average batch size, error rate (500s/4xx)

Design/asset notes for the deck conversion
- Diagram: simple two-tone flow, annotate with three colored hotspots: cache, batch, fallback. Export as svg.
- Slide visuals: use one full-bleed diagram slide and one small table slide with sample pilot KPIs.
- Placeholder filenames: diagram-request-flow.svg, pilot-kpi-table.png, battlecard-onepager.pdf

Sample email blurb for AE/SE to use when asking for pilot materials:
"Quick ask: can you share a 24–48 hour sample of traffic (anonymized), and a small set of 30 representative prompts and the expected output? We’ll run a 1-week pilot that measures latency, cache hit rate, and token spend — typical customers see the biggest wins when repeated prefixes are >20% of traffic."

Open questions / things to confirm in engineering sync
- Minimum instrumentation we require from customer to measure real improvement? (e.g., do they need header propagation for trace id?)
- Default canary config for new integrations: percent ramp steps, rollback heuristics, alerting thresholds.
- Where to place the per-route eval harness (customer side, or central Redwood job)?

Quick experimental ideas (brainstormed)
- "prefix-sampler": capture 1% of requests to sample longer contexts and compute potential cacheable prefixes offline. Useful for quick ROI estimate.
- Auto-suggest model variant based on request tail latency and cost budgets per route.

Notes to self (TODOs)
- Convert this doc to a 6-slide draft by EOD Tuesday.
- Pair with design to render diagram and a compact battlecard PDF.
- Sync with product: confirm latest quantization guidance and provide slide with benchmark numbers.

References / bookmarks
- Pilot runbook (internal): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/Pilot+Runbook
- Model catalog summary: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ML/Model+Catalog

End.
